questions.q: Describe how to find the percentage of oxygen in air using iron wool (or copper and syringes), and explain the result. Portal response box.
questions.a: Known volume of air (1); iron wool in a measuring cylinder over water (1); leave several days (1); iron rusts, using oxygen (1); water rises; measure volume change (1); about 21% (1).
questions.model: Teacher writes the first two points: 'Push damp iron wool to the bottom of a measuring cylinder and invert it in water. Record the starting volume of air.'

questions.q: Explain why aluminium does not seem as reactive as its position suggests.
questions.a: Aluminium has a protective oxide layer (1) that stops air and water reaching the metal (1), so it reacts slowly (1).

questions.q: Write a balanced equation for sodium reacting with water.
Predict how rubidium reacts with water.
questions.a: Very vigorously, more than potassium (1); forms rubidium hydroxide and hydrogen (1).
questions.model: Trend: reactivity increases down Group 1. Rubidium is below potassium, so it reacts even more violently. Products: metal hydroxide and hydrogen.

questions.q: Use the grid to put Mg, Zn and Cu in order of reactivity.

questions.a: Zinc coating is a barrier to air and water (1); zinc is more reactive so corrodes first even if scratched (1).

questions.q: Big question: why is potassium stored under oil but gold found as metal?
questions.a: Potassium is very reactive and would react with air and water; gold is unreactive so it stays uncombined.
